name: Phaeochromocytoma crisis

matching.reasoningTemplate: Episodic headache, palpitations and sweating with paroxysmal hypertension suggests a catecholamine-secreting tumour.

redFlags: Paroxysmal severe hypertension — alpha-blockade before beta

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e — referenced across chapters: hypertension (book p.2140-2141), cardiomyopathy/heart failure, palpitations, cancer genetics, cardiac tumors, mastocytosis; dedicated pheochromocytoma chapter (Ch. 399, book p.3073)
clinicalPearls: The classic triad is episodic headache, palpitations and sweating (diaphoresis) occurring with paroxysmal hypertension (p.2140).
Most patients present with hypertension at a relatively young age, often between 30 and 50 years (p.2140).
Many patients have only non-specific symptoms; the florid paroxysmal presentation is not universal, so the diagnosis is easily missed (p.2140).
Catecholamine-secreting tumours arise from chromaffin cells: roughly 80-85% are in the adrenal medulla, the remainder being extra-adrenal paraganglioma in paraganglion tissue (p.2140).
Patients with pheochromocytoma frequently have postural (orthostatic) hypotension despite the hypertension, reflecting volume contraction and impaired sympathetic reflexes (cardiomyopathy chapter).
Catecholamine excess can produce a hyperdynamic state and palpitations, and is one of the recognised endocrine causes alongside thyrotoxicosis and mastocytosis (palpitations chapter).
harrison.pathophysiology: Excess production of catecholamines, usually by a benign neuroendocrine tumour of chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla (80-85%) or in extra-adrenal paraganglion tissue (paraganglioma). The catecholamine surge drives paroxysmal hypertension, headache, sweating and cardiac arrhythmias, and produces a hyperdynamic catecholaminergic state. Chronic/episodic catecholamine exposure can cause microvascular myocardial ischaemia (microinfarcts similar to those seen with stimulant toxicity) and a catecholamine-mediated cardiomyopathy; the same mechanism of sudden catecholamine release underlies stress (takotsubo / apical ballooning) cardiomyopathy (hypertension, cardiomyopathy and cardiac-tumour chapters).
additionalDifferentials: Cushing's syndrome and other secondary causes of hypertension (more common than pheochromocytoma, so the classic triad is frequently misleading) (p.2140).
Thyrotoxicosis / hyperthyroidism (overlapping palpitations, sweating, tremor; an endocrine cause of palpitations) (palpitations chapter).
Panic / anxiety disorder and somatization (episodic palpitations, sweating, sense of doom mimicking paroxysms) (palpitations chapter).
Stimulant toxicity — cocaine, amphetamines and related catecholaminergic drugs (produce hypertension, tachyarrhythmia, microvascular ischaemia resembling pheochromocytoma) (cardiomyopathy chapter).
Systemic mastocytosis / mast-cell activation (flushing, palpitations, hypotensive episodes) (mastocytosis chapter).
nonInfectiousMimics: Systemic mastocytosis — flushing and palpitation attacks; urinary metanephrines help exclude pheochromocytoma when evaluating mast-cell symptoms (mastocytosis chapter).
Carcinoid tumour — overlapping flushing/paroxysmal symptoms; assessed together with metanephrines in differential testing (mastocytosis chapter).
Stimulant (cocaine/amphetamine) toxicity producing a catecholaminergic crisis with hypertension and arrhythmia (cardiomyopathy chapter).
Takotsubo (stress / apical ballooning) cardiomyopathy — catecholamine-mediated, can follow a surge resembling pheochromocytoma (cardiac trauma / cardiomyopathy chapters).
additionalInvestigations: Blood and 24-hour urinary catecholamine measurement (in addition to plasma/urine metanephrines) (p.2140).
Functional/positron emission tomography (PET) imaging in addition to CT/MRI of the abdomen for localisation (p.2140).
Nuclear localisation with 131-I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scanning, e.g. for extra-adrenal/cardiac paraganglioma (cardiac-tumour chapter).
Genetic evaluation when a hereditary predisposition is suspected (MEN2/RET, von Hippel-Lindau, neurofibromatosis type 1, hereditary paraganglioma syndromes) (p.2140).
redFlags: Pheochromocytoma in crisis is named alongside aortic dissection and eclampsia as a hypertensive emergency demanding particularly rapid management; control blood pressure with a titratable IV agent (p.2141).
Very labile blood pressure and heart rate with episodic palpitations occurring together with new heart failure should raise suspicion of pheochromocytoma (cardiomyopathy chapter).
Coexisting postural hypotension with paroxysmal hypertension is a clue to catecholamine excess rather than essential hypertension (cardiomyopathy chapter).
harrison.prognosis: A benign tumour is usual; definitive treatment is surgical extirpation (complete or partial adrenalectomy, typically minimally invasive), which is generally curative. Surgery requires prior alpha-adrenergic receptor blockade. Untreated catecholamine excess can precipitate hypertensive emergency, arrhythmia, catecholamine cardiomyopathy and heart failure (hypertension and cardiomyopathy chapters).
pitfalls: Representativeness-heuristic trap: clinicians overestimate the probability of pheochromocytoma when the classic headache-palpitations-sweating triad is present, because they neglect its low prevalence relative to common causes of hypertension; the triad also occurs in patients who do not have the tumour (clinical-reasoning chapter, p.~? — diagnostic reasoning).
Conversely, non-specific or atypical presentations can lead to the diagnosis being missed entirely (clinical-reasoning chapter).
Postural hypotension may be wrongly attributed to over-treatment of hypertension rather than recognised as a catecholamine-excess clue (cardiomyopathy chapter).
